How Reproducibility Check works

This module assesses whether a paper’s R and Python code can be run on its data. It works in two phases. The static phase (always run) collects the package dependencies the code declares, rewrites the data-file paths that do not work in the repository as the authors organised it, works out the order the scripts must run in, and diagnoses why any referenced input file is unavailable — reporting what a reproduction attempt would involve and where it is likely to break. The execution phase (opt-in, execute = TRUE) then actually runs the code: it copies the repository into a throwaway directory, optionally installs the declared dependencies into a throwaway library, runs each script in order in an isolated subprocess with a per-script timeout, and captures the outcome and full output of each run.

By default (execute = FALSE) the module does not run any code — it performs only static analysis: reading dependencies with the same extractors as code_check, finding the files the code references in the repository, and building a run-order dependency graph. It reports what would be installed and run rather than doing it.

When execute = TRUE, the module additionally runs the downloaded code on your machine — a deliberate, opt-in action gated behind that argument (callr is required for R code). Each script runs in an isolated subprocess so a crash cannot take down the R session; note this isolates crashes, not the filesystem or network. Installs (when install_missing = TRUE) and the throwaway run library never touch your main R library. Each script’s outcome is one of ran_ok, errored, timed_out, dependency_unavailable, not_parsed, run_by_source (an R script another script runs with source(), which is run only inside that script, since on its own it lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first), run_by_import (a Python file other files import, a module rather than a script, unless it has an if __name__ == "__main__": block), jags_model (a JAGS or BUGS model saved with an R extension, which another script reads) or not_r_content (a file that is not R at all, such as a JSON or HTML dump); these last two are not run and are not failures. python2 marks Python 2 code that was not run. With sandbox = "docker" such code runs with Python 2.7 (option metacheck.docker_image_py2; FALSE turns this off), which modifications records; it is never converted, since that can change results. defines_functions is a file that only defines functions, which is used, not run (table$used_by names the scripts that use it), and not_analysis is a file of software rather than of the analysis: a package’s code, tests, documentation or setup.py, a copy of a tool, a web application, a script a program wrote (table$not_analysis_why says which); neither is run or counted as a script. docker_failed means the container never started, which says nothing about the script, so it keeps the light from being green but does not make it red. needs_a_person is a script that stopped because it asks a person to choose a file or answer a question, or that starts an app, and needs_internet one that stopped because the network is off in a Docker run, or, with internet = TRUE, could not reach what it asked for; download_too_large is a script stopped for downloading more than the limits allow (see internet), and out_of_memory one that, or a program it started (such as a compiler), ran out of the memory each script may use. All four are treated the same way. not_downloaded is a script that stopped on a file the repository lists but that was not downloaded, such as one over max_file_size: it could not be tried, so it is not counted as a script that did not reproduce (summary_table$repro_not_downloaded_n counts them apart). not_read is a file metacheck could not read, so it was not run; the light is then not green, as the file may read and run on another computer, and table$error_message says why, naming a package that is installed but cannot be loaded on the computer that ran the check. empty is a file with nothing in it, which is not run or counted as a script. For a script that did not run through, table$error_message is its error, short (at most 300 characters): the error line of its output, which names a package that is not there, with the address it asked for when it needed the internet, or the time limit it reached; table$reason sorts it into a kind. A timeout means “still running at the cutoff”, not a failure, so raise timeout for legitimately long-running (e.g. Bayesian) scripts. dependency_unavailable means the script’s own package could not be installed from live CRAN, the CRAN Archive, or a named GitHub/URL source — an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code. The full stdout/stderr of every run is kept in the result’s run_results (the report shows it in per-script dropdowns, capped for readability).

Provenance, kept so that a TRACE Research Object (TRO) declaration of the run can be written later from a stored result (metacheck #404; the helpers are in R/provenance.R). Only when code was run (execute = TRUE): * run_results$started_at, run_results$ended_at: when each run of a script started and ended (ISO 8601, UTC, milliseconds); NA for a script that was not started. A script run again in a later pass has the times of its last run. A TRO uses them for each trov:TransparentResearchPerformance. * run_results$exit_status: the exit status of the process that ran the script (0 = ended normally); NA when the process did not report one (a time limit, or Docker failing to start the container). * artifacts: one row per file, with stage (deposit: as downloaded from the repository, hashed from the downloaded file; before_run: the run folder just before the first script ran, after metacheck’s own changes, such as rewritten paths and unpacked archives; after_run: only the files the scripts made (status new), changed (changed) or removed (removed), as an unchanged file is the one listed before the run), path (relative to the run folder, as valid UTF-8, a byte of another encoding written as <xx>), size (bytes), sha256, mime_type (by extension, NA when unknown), source (the file’s address in the repository, for deposit). The package libraries metacheck installs in the run folder are left out, as are metacheck’s own files there (a script’s runner, and the statistical output it writes in statistical_output/). Files metacheck itself copied or made between passes (see modifications, output_copied, file_placed) show in after_run too. A TRO uses the rows as trov:ResearchArtifacts and each stage as a trov:ArtifactArrangement. * modifications$sha256_before, modifications$sha256_after: the hash of the changed script as downloaded and as it ran; NA when the script is not at the same path in both (a script made from an R Markdown file). * environment: the system that ran the code (trov:TransparentResearchSystem in a TRO): metacheck_version, started_at, ended_at, host (R version, platform, operating system), sandbox, network_isolated (TRUE only when every Docker run had --network none; the process sandbox does not stop the network), internet, timeout_per_script, total_timeout, python_local (the Python run outside Docker and its version), and docker: runs (for each kind of run, r_run, r_install, python_run, python_install, the image and the docker run arguments, such as --network none, --read-only, --cap-drop ALL, no-new-privileges, the process limit and the memory and processor limits) and images (for each image, its ID and digests from docker image inspect, its creation time and the R and Python versions its environment declares).

run_results$checked says what the run of each script shows about the code, in five groups, so that a script that does not reproduce is kept apart from one the check could not test: ran (it ran to the end); code_error (it did not reproduce: it stopped with an error of the code or the deposit, could not be read, or needs a file the deposit does not hold); dependency (a package or program was not available: a package that could not be installed or was not loaded, a program outside R and Python, a system library, or R crashing in a package’s compiled code); time (it did not finish within the time limit for one script, or was not started because the time for all scripts had run out); and not_checkable (it could not be checked automatically: it needs a person, the internet, a key or another setting of the authors’ computer, one platform such as Google Colab, Windows or OpenSAFELY, more memory than the run allows, a file that was not downloaded, a screen, or a program that runs it, or it is a file of a package of the code that Python runs only as a module of that package). It is NA for files run inside another script, files that are not an analysis, files not read, and a Docker failure. summary_table counts each group (repro_ran_n, repro_code_error_n, repro_dependency_n, repro_time_n, repro_not_checkable_n), and the report’s first sentence gives them. The traffic light reflects the static readiness signals by default; a script in code_error that stopped with an error makes it red, as a script that crashes on its own analysis is a genuine reproduction failure, and a script in one of the other three groups keeps it from being green. Calls that need a screen, which the run does not have (dev.print(), dev.copy2pdf(), dev.copy2eps(), savePlot(), windows(), win.graph(), x11(), quartz(), View()), are replaced before the run by calls that need none, which modifications records as screen_call_replaced. A script that fails with could not find function is run once more with the library() calls the project’s other scripts make added at its top (or the one package that exports the function, or magrittr for %>%), and a script that then runs is reported as reproducible only after that repair.

Dependencies are reported name-only, with the source (CRAN, GitHub, or a base package already shipped with R) — static analysis of the code cannot know which version was used, and running against current package versions is itself informative: a break argues the authors should have pinned versions. When the repository does record versions, a run with recorded_versions = TRUE installs the packages the scripts load at those versions, but it does not change the R version, which remains a limitation of the check.

Run order is derived from read-after-write data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads must run first), source() edges, and numeric filename prefixes as a weak tie-breaker. Ambiguous orderings, dependency cycles, and inputs a script reads but that no earlier script produces (and that are not in the repository) are surfaced as warnings, since these are the situations most likely to make an otherwise-correct reproduction fail.

Python code (.py files, and notebooks and Quarto documents whose code is Python, from which the code is extracted first) goes through the same two phases, reported in its own “Python code” section. Each file is checked for syntax errors with Python’s own parser when a Python interpreter (python, or else python3) is available; dependencies are read from the import statements, with versions from a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml when there is one, and installed with pip; each script runs as its own python process (processx is required), so unlike R scripts, a name one script defines is not available to another. When no Python interpreter is available, the Python files are reported as not run and the R results are still returned. Statistics the Python scripts print are compared with the paper together with the R output and any self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, notebook outputs).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited. No reminder is given when the paper already cites that replication or reproduction (matched by its DOI).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

We want to thank Zuzana Štěrbová for her help and advice in preparing the survey. This study would not have been possible without the help of various LGBTQ+ and other associations, including social media-based pages and influencers who helped with the recruitment of participants

INTRODUCTION

Previous research has identified several personality differences among people with various sexual orientations, mainly focusing on gay/lesbian and heterosexual men and women (for meta-analyses, see Allen & Robson, 2020 and Allen & Walter, 2018), and sometimes including also bisexual people (see Allen & Robson, 2020). Only a handful of studies also included asexual (i.e., no sexual attraction to other people; Bogaert, 2015) and pansexual (i.e., attraction to other people regardless of their sex or gender; Junkins et al., 2024) people in their research samples.

These previous studies mainly employed the so-called Big Five model (Costa & McCrae, 1992), which is one of the most widely used personality models today and describes human personality at the highest level of abstraction. It comprises five factors identified through factor analysis of personality adjectives occurring in natural language (e.g., Norman, 1963). The five-factor structure has also been independently confirmed using other methodological approaches (Costa & McCrae, 1992). Czech belongs among the languages with a confirmed five-factor structure (Hřebíčková, 1999). These five factors include neuroticism (which refers to proneness to anxiety, depressiveness, and psychological vulnerability), extraversion (warmth, sociability), agreeableness (trustfulness, tendency to altruism), conscientiousness (dependableness, tendency to be organized), and openness to experience (intellectual curiosity, preference for novelty).

Previous studies found that both gay and bisexual men score constantly higher in neuroticism than heterosexual men (for meta-analyses, see Allen & Robson, 2020, and Allen & Walter, 2018). One of two studies also reported higher neuroticism in asexual men (Carvalho et al., 2017 , but see Bogaert et al., 2018, for no difference). In women, some studies found bisexual women scoring higher in neuroticism than heterosexual women (Allen & Robson, 2020, but see Bogaert et al., 2018, for no difference). However, there are no consistent results regarding differences in neuroticism between heterosexual and lesbian women. One meta-analysis found lower neuroticism in lesbians (Allen & Walter, 2018), while the other meta-analysis observed no significant differences (Allen & Robson, 2020; see also Greaves et al., 2017; Peixoto & Nobre, 2016). One study found higher neuroticism (Carvalho et al., 2017), and another one lower neuroticism in asexual women in comparison with heterosexual women (Bogaert et al., 2018). In two studies that employed mixed-sex samples, one found higher neuroticism in asexual compared to heterosexual individuals (Greaves et al., 2021), whereas the other found no difference (Junkins et al., 2024). To our knowledge, the only study to date that included pansexual individuals found higher neuroticism in pansexual compared to heterosexual individuals (regardless of their gender; Junkins et al., 2024).

No consistent differences were found in extraversion among gay and heterosexual men (Allen & Robson, 2020; Allen & Walter, 2018) or among bisexual and heterosexual men (Allen & Robson, 2020). In women, one meta-analysis found no difference (Allen & Walter, 2018), but the other found lower extraversion in both bisexual and lesbian compared to heterosexual women (Allen & Robson, 2020). In contrast, there is unequivocal evidence that asexual men and women (Bogaert et al., 2018; Carvalho et al., 2017) or asexual individuals regardless of their gender (Greaves et al., 2021; Junkins et al., 2024) have lower extraversion than heterosexual individuals. No differences were found between pansexual and heterosexual individuals (Junkins et al., 2024).

Most of the studies reported that non-heterosexual individuals score higher in openness to experience than their heterosexual counterparts. This holds for gay men, bisexual men, lesbian women, and bisexual women, as was clearly demonstrated by two metaanalyses (Allen & Robson, 2020; Allen & Walter, 2018; but see Sadr-Bazzaz et al., 2024, for null results). Asexual men scored higher in openness than heterosexual men (Bogaert et al., 2018; Carvalho et al., 2017), and one study recorded higher openness also in asexual women as compared to heterosexual women (Bogaert et al., 2018 , but see Carvalho et al., 2017, for null results). Greaves et al. (2021) reported higher openness in asexual people in a mixed-sex sample. Pansexual people were also found to be higher in openness than heterosexuals (Junkins et al., 2024).

Regarding conscientiousness, the results of studies are ambiguous. One meta-analysis found no difference between heterosexual and gay men (Allen & Walter, 2018), while the other recorded lower conscientiousness in heterosexual men (Allen & Robson, 2020; see also Peixoto and Nobre, 2016, who found higher conscientiousness in heterosexual men). Lesbian women were observed to score lower in conscientiousness in one meta-analysis (Allen & Robson, 2020), while the other found no difference (Allen & Walter, 2018). Bisexual women, as well as bisexual men, were found to be lower on conscientiousness than both heterosexual and gay/lesbian women and men (Allen & Robson, 2020). Asexual women were found lower on this trait than heterosexual women (Bogaert et al., 2018; Carvalho et al., 2017); asexual and heterosexual men showed no or minimal differences (Bogaert et al., 2018; Carvalho et al., 2017). Pansexual individuals showed lower conscientiousness than heterosexual individuals (Junkins et al., 2024).

Finally, no consistent differences were found in the level of agreeableness among gay, bisexual, and heterosexual men, with both meta-analyses observing no discernible differences (Allen & Robson, 2020; Allen & Walter, 2018 , but see Lippa, 2008). Some studies recorded lower agreeableness in lesbian women than in heterosexual women (Allen & Robson, 2020, but see Allen & Walter, 2018, for null results). Bisexual women were found to be less agreeable than heterosexual women (Allen & Robson, 2020; Bogaert et al., 2018). Asexual individuals, on average, do not differ in agreeableness from heterosexual individuals (Bogaert et al., 2018; Carvalho et al., 2017; Junkins et al., 2024), but one study recorded lower agreeableness in asexual individuals (Greaves et al., 2021). Pansexual did not differ in agreeableness from heterosexual individuals (Junkins et al., 2024).

Possible Mechanisms Driving Personality Differences

Researchers have proposed multiple mechanisms that could be responsible for these personality differences among people of various sexual orientations. One explanation might stem from the so-called gender shift in non-heterosexual individuals (see LeVay, 2017).

According to the gender shift hypothesis, sexual orientation is a result of hormonal influences during prenatal development. The sex-atypical prenatal and perinatal level of sex steroids, primarily androgens (Swift-Gallant et al., 2022), is hypothesized to "shift" the development of some individuals so they resemble their other-sex counterparts in many respects, including sexual attraction. Indeed, there is evidence that gay/lesbian individuals are shifted in many physical traits, including the length of limbs (Martin & Nguyen, 2004), body height (Bogaert, 2003), or finger length ratios (Aguilar, 2023), all of which are under the influence of sex steroids. Non-heterosexual individuals are, on average, also more gender nonconforming than heterosexual individuals; bisexual and gay men show feminine-like occupational preferences (Lippa, 2008; Zheng et al., 2011), childhood sex-typed behavior (Rieger et al., 2008), or partner height preference (Valentova et al., 2016), while bisexual and lesbian women show masculine-like occupational preferences and childhood sex-typed behavior (Lippa, 2008; Rieger et al., 2008; Valentova et al., 2016; Zheng et al., 2011).

At least some of the personality differences existing among individuals of various sexual orientations could be another manifestation of this gender shift. For instance, a largescale study based on 55 samples worldwide revealed small but consistent sex differences in the Big Five traits (Schmitt et al., 2008)-neuroticism (d = 0.40, women higher than men), agreeableness (d = 0.15, W > M), conscientiousness (d = 0.12, W > M), extraversion (d = 0.10, W > M), and openness (d = 0.05, M > W). As the most marked difference pertained to neuroticism, we would expect to see higher neuroticism in non-heterosexual men and lower neuroticism in non-heterosexual women, if the gender shift was in play.

Another mechanism which may contribute to the differences in personality characteristics is minority stress which is experienced by non-heterosexual individuals. The minority stress theory asserts that mental health disparities between sexual minorities and heterosexual people arise from increased exposure to social stress linked to the marginalized social position of sexual minorities (Meyer, 2003). Minority stressors can be distal, referring to external actions by individuals or institutions-such as discriminatory state policies or unfair treatment due to minority sexual orientation-or proximal, referring to internal psychological consequences of living in a predominantly heterosexual society, such as internalized stigma or expectations of rejection (Frost & Meyer, 2023). Indeed, compared with heterosexual people, non-heterosexual individuals face a higher risk of suicidality and self-harm (Swannell et al., 2016), depression and anxiety (Borgogna et al., 2019), and substance abuse (Drabble et al., 2018). A recent meta-analysis of 26 studies conducted across diverse geographic regions found that, overall, gay/lesbian participants had twice the odds of experiencing depression, suicidality, anxiety disorders, and alcohol use disorders compared to heterosexual participants (Wittgens et al., 2022). Moreover, one study found that disparities in well-being vary across countries, with differences in structural stigma at the national level accounting for 60% of the cross-national variation in well-being gaps (Pachankis & Bränström, 2018). According to the minority stress theory, we would expect to see higher neuroticism (as neuroticism is also defined by negative affectivity and emotional instability) in all marginalized non-heterosexual groups compared to heterosexual individuals.

In general, non-heterosexual individuals live to some extent in a different social reality than heterosexuals. For instance, the awareness of already breaking the societal expectations about other-sex sexuality, non-heterosexual individuals may find it easier than heterosexual individuals to be open to various other kinds of experiences, which would manifest in their higher openness to experience (Bogaert et al., 2018).

Last but not least, there is a heritable genetic component to both sexual orientation (Ganna et al., 2019) and the Big Five personality traits (Vukasović & Bratko, 2015). The same genes could influence both sexual orientation and personality, as was already suggested for neuroticism (Zietsch et al., 2011).

Current Study

In this online study, we build upon the previous research implementing the Big Five model of personality. Previous studies were primarily based on samples from Englishspeaking countries (Allen & Robson, 2020); for notable exceptions see Bozkurt et al. (2006), Carvalho et al. (2017), or Ifrah et al. (2018). Our main aim is to replicate previous (see our predictions below) Big Five differences in a novel non-English speaking sample, expanding substantially the standard scope by including also self-identified asexual and pansexual individuals along with gay/lesbian, heterosexual, and bisexual cisgender participants. Czechia and Slovakia are Central European countries with a largely homogenous ethnic population and a large share of non-believers (over 50 % of population in Czechia) (Vachuška & Kurkin, 2022) and a relatively low levels of homophobia (Lamontagne et al., 2018; see also Pitoňák & Spilková, 2016).

Based on the research reviewed above, we had three main predictions. First, heterosexual men will score lower in neuroticism than men of any other sexual orientationsthis is predicted both by the minority stress and the gender shift frameworks. As the minority stress theory would predict higher, but gender shift lower neuroticism in non-heterosexual women, we had no specific predictions about neuroticism differences among women. Second, both heterosexual men and women will score lower in openness to experience than their same-sex counterparts of any other sexual orientations. Third, asexual men and women will score lower in extraversion than their same-sex heterosexual counterparts-this prediction is mainly data-driven based on past empirical work. We had no specific predictions about agreeableness and conscientiousness because previous studies gained no consistent results.

METHODS

We report how we determined our sample size, all data exclusions (if any), all manipulations, and all measures in the study. Adherence to TOP guidelines is appended as a checklist at the end of this preprint (Appendix A).

Participants

The data reported here are part of a larger project that was called (and publicly communicated as) "Sexual orientation, personality, and attractiveness." A total of 10,312 respondents initiated the online survey. Sessions of those who did not provide informed consent (N = 98) or indicated an age lower than 18 years (N = 112) were terminated. To increase the credibility of the analyzed data, we further excluded participants who (1) were older than 59 years (as outliers; N = 26), (2) stopped responding before finishing initial sociodemographic questions (N = 1,423), (3) claimed they have ten or more maternal or paternal aunts or uncles (considered unlikely based on Czech demographics; N = 18), (4) claimed to have ten or more offspring (which we again considered unlikely; N = 3), (5) provided an obviously non-serious label for sex or gender (N = 11; e.g., "attack helicopter").

We further excluded those who (6) responded to individual psychological scales in a manifestly negligent manner-e.g., by choosing the extreme option for each item, although some were reverse-coded (N = 23). We note that five people met (and are counted in) more than one exclusion criterion. The cutoff of 59 years was selected as a compromise between reducing age-related variation in sexual identification (Twenge et al., 2024) and avoiding the exclusion of an unnecessarily large proportion of our participants.

In the dataset, there were 3,399 cisgender men (male sex assigned at birth with male gender identity) and 4,573 cisgender women (female sex assigned at birth with female gender identity). Eight participants who indicated sex as "other" (not to be confused with transgender people), 110 non-cisgender male (male sex assigned at birth) and 513 non-cisgender female (female sex assigned at birth) participants were omitted from analyses. We took this measure because we could not tell whether these non-cisgender participants' self-identified sexual orientation (see below) refer to their current gender or sex, or their partner's gender or sex. Of the remaining count, 2,816 men and 3,969 women provided complete data on the Big Five.

The final male sample (see Table 1) consisted of 822 cisgender men self-identified as heterosexual, 1,522 as gay, 353 as bisexual, 44 as pansexual, and 13 as asexual. Twenty-two men chose the option "other," and 40 men chose "I do not know" to describe their sexual orientation; those were omitted from analyses. The final female sample consisted of 1,776 individuals identified as heterosexual, 421 as lesbian, 1,059 as bisexual, 345 as pansexual, and 121 as asexual. Eighty-six women chose the option "other," and 161 women chose "I do not know" to describe their sexual orientation; those were omitted from analyses.

Sociodemographic descriptives are to be found in Table 1.

Recruitment and Procedure

The data collection spanned between November 2022 and February 2023. The only condition to participate in the study was age above 18 years. The study was broadcasted through social media by asking various LGBT+ targeted and other (LGBT+ non-targeted) web pages and influencers to share the link to the survey. The study was further promoted on Meta Platforms, Inc. Concurrently, we placed printed leaflets with QR codes linked to the survey at various university buildings, libraries, and some other public places, mainly in Prague. The online survey was administered on the Qualtrics platform in the Czech language, and its completion took approximately 30-40 minutes (Mdn = 29 minutes). The participants were informed that the study aims "to explore a range of psychological, personality, and family characteristics associated with (non-)heterosexual orientation" and that their answers are strictly confidential, will be anonymized, and that they can withdraw from the study anytime. Subsequently, they provided informed consent by ticking a checkbox and were administered a battery of self-reported measures, and upon completion, thanked and debriefed.

Participants received no compensation for taking part in the study. All procedures were conducted in accordance with the Helsinki Declaration. The study was approved by the review board of Charles University, Faculty of Science (August 10, 2022; No. 2022/23).

Measures

The complete list of measures is provided in Supplementary Material. Below, we describe only measures relevant to the current study.

There was an initial section of sociodemographic items. Those relevant to this research included age, sex assigned at birth, gender identity, nationality, highest education achieved, and population size of present residence. Choices for the gender item included (listed as adjectives): Male, female, non-binary, and other. For a list of choices for the remaining sociodemographic items, see Table 1.

We assessed sexual orientation by asking the participants: "What is your sexual orientation?" with a provided set of labels/choices: Homosexual, heterosexual, bisexual, pansexual, asexual, I do not know, or other 1.

The Big Five personality traits were assessed by the official Czech version (Hřebíčková et al., 2016) of the 10-item Big Five Inventory (BFI-10; Rammstedt & John, 2007)-the original English version of this short scale showed validity estimates sufficient for research settings (Rammstedt & John, 2007). Each trait was assessed by two items like "I see myself as someone who… gets nervous easily" for neuroticism or "… is outgoing, sociable" for extraversion, and participants indicated a degree of their agreement on a 5-point scale ("disagree strongly" to "agree strongly"). Scores of two items were summed to obtain the total score for each trait. A higher score indicates a higher level of a particular trait. By the recommendation of Eisinga et al. (2013) for two-item scales, we calculated the reliability using the Spearman-Brown formula for each trait-neuroticism (ρ = 0.72), extraversion (ρ = 0.58), conscientiousness (ρ = 0.45), openness (ρ = 0.33), and agreeableness (ρ = 0.17). These values are comparable to those obtained in a Czech validation study (Hřebíčková et al., 2016).

Power Analysis

Our primary aim was to recruit as many participants as possible before the end of the predetermined data collection period, which concluded in February 2023. For power estimation related to our first prediction-that heterosexual men would score lower in 1 Czech equivalents of English labels were provided, i.e.: Homosexuální, heterosexuální, bisexuální, pansexuální, asexuální, jiná, nevím. The five sexual identity labels share the same etymological origin as their English equivalents and are understood and commonly used in the Czech language. neuroticism than men of any other sexual orientation-and our second prediction-that heterosexual men and women would score lower in openness than their same-sex counterparts of other sexual orientations-we used effect sizes reported by Allen and Robson (2020) in their meta-analysis of convenience samples. These were d = 0.4 for neuroticism differences among men and d = 0.3 for openness differences among both men and women.

As Allen and Robson (2020) reported differences only between gay/lesbian / heterosexual and bisexual/heterosexual individuals, and given the limited data on personality differences in pansexual and asexual populations, we assumed these effect sizes would also apply to comparisons between heterosexual individuals and asexual or pansexual individuals. For our third prediction-that asexual men and women would score lower in extraversion than heterosexual men and women-we used effect sizes from the largest study to date on asexual individuals (Bogaert et al., 2018), which reported d = 0.8 for both men and women.

Based on these effect sizes, we conducted a priori power analyses for pairwise comparisons between two independent groups (two-tailed α = 0.05, 1-β = 0.80) 2 . Assuming equal group sizes, the required total sample sizes were N = 200 for the first prediction, N = 352 for the second, and N = 52 for the third. Given the actual unequal group sizes (see Participants), we did not achieve sufficient power for comparing neuroticism scores between pansexual and heterosexual men (observed power 1-β = 0.73, assuming d = 0.4 and α = 0.05), asexual and heterosexual men (observed power 1-β = 0.30, assuming d = 0.4 and α = 0.05), openness scores between pansexual and heterosexual men (observed power 1-β = 0.49, assuming d = 0.3 and α = 0.05), or openness scores between asexual and heterosexual men (observed power 1-β = 0.19, assuming d = 0.3 and α = 0.05). Sufficient power (1-β ≥ 0.80) 2 As examining Big Five differences across sexual orientations was not a primary aim of our project, these power analyses were computed after data collection was completed.

was achieved for all other predicted pairwise comparisons. All power calculations were performed using G*Power (version 3.1.9.7).

Data Analysis

The data were prepared in Excel and analyzed in Jamovi (The Jamovi Project, 2024).

Color figure was prepared in RStudio (Posit team, 2026). We first assessed the normality of the Big Five traits and age by using the Shapiro-Wilk test and found a significant deviation from normality in all variables (all ps < .001). We, therefore, used non-parametric tests in all subsequent analyses. Since we were not interested in cross-sex comparisons (and were interested in comparisons among orientations within each sex), all analyses were performed separately for men and women to increase the power of pairwise within-sex comparisons. We conducted a series of Kruskal-Wallis (KW) tests, with each personality trait as a dependent variable and sexual orientation as an independent variable. If the overall model was formally significant, each KW test was followed by Dwass-Steel-Critchlow-Fligner (DSCF) pairwise comparisons. To assess age-related fluctuations, we conducted bivariate Spearman crosscorrelations between each personality trait and age. If we found that the personality trait was significantly associated with age, we would run a linear regression with a given personality trait as a dependent variable and age as a predictor. Residuals obtained from the regression would then be utilized as a dependent variable in another KW test to control for the possible effect of age on intergroup differences. Between-group differences in age were tested using KW test followed by DSCF pairwise comparisons. The alpha level for statistical significance (hereinafter "significance") was set to 0.05. The data (Fořt et al., 2026a) and code (Fořt et al., 2026b) associated with this research are available publicly: https://osf.io/vt2yx/files/osfstorage.

RESULTS

In men, we found significant correlations between age and neuroticism (ρ = -.08), extraversion (ρ = .04), and conscientiousness (ρ = .15). In women, we recorded significant correlations between age and neuroticism (ρ = -.18), extraversion (ρ = .08), and conscientiousness (ρ = .16). All bivariate correlations are reported in Table 2. KW test for age differences in men (H(4) = 51.99, p < .001, ε2 = 0.02) showed that gay men were significantly older than bisexual (d = 0.15), heterosexual (d = 0.17), and pansexual (d = 0.58) men, and that pansexual men were significantly younger than heterosexual (d = 0.41) and bisexual men (d = 0.44). Similarly for women (H(4) = 128.87, p < .001, ε2 = 0.03), lesbian and heterosexual women were significantly older than asexual (d = 0.47, d = 0.45), bisexual (d = 0.39, d = 0.37), and pansexual (d = 0.40, d = 0.38) women. No other between-group age differences were found.

In men, KW tests indicated significant differences in neuroticism, extraversion, openness, and conscientiousness. For descriptive statistics, see Table 3; for model specifications and pairwise comparisons, see Table 4. The differences among men are plotted in Figure 1. Heterosexual men scored significantly lower in neuroticism than bisexual (d = 0.19) and gay (d = 0.26) men, and bisexual men scored lower than pansexual (d = 0.47) men.

Asexual men scored lower in extraversion than heterosexual (d = 0.79), bisexual (d = 0.94), gay (d = 0.99), and pansexual (d = 1.09) men. Gay men scored higher than heterosexual (d = 0.20) men. Heterosexual men scored lower in openness than pansexual (d = 0.45) and bisexual (d = 0.18) men. Heterosexual men showed lower levels of conscientiousness than bisexual (d = 0.21) and gay (d = 0.25) men, who showed higher levels of conscientiousness than pansexual (d = 0.43) men. We did not observe any significant differences in agreeableness based on sexual orientation.

In women, KW tests indicated significant differences in neuroticism, extraversion, openness, and conscientiousness. For descriptive statistics, see Table 3; for model specifications and pairwise comparisons, see Table 4. The differences among women are plotted in Figure 1. Heterosexual women scored lower in neuroticism than bisexual (d = 0.13) and pansexual (d = 0.15) women. Similarly, lesbian women scored lower than bisexual (d = 0.24), asexual (d = 0.31), and pansexual (d = 0.26) women. Asexual women scored lower in extraversion than heterosexual (d = 0.73), bisexual (d = 0.72), lesbian (d = 0.77), and pansexual (d = 0.73) women. Pansexual women scored higher in openness than heterosexual (d = 0.50), bisexual (d = 0.21), lesbian (d = 0.45), and asexual (d = 0.45) women. Furthermore, bisexual women scored higher than heterosexual (d = 0.29) and lesbian (d = 0.25) women. Heterosexual women scored higher in conscientiousness than bisexual (d = 0.30), asexual (d = 0.31), and pansexual (d = 0.24) women. Lesbian women scored higher than bisexual (d = 0.25) women. As was the case in men, we did not record statistically significant differences in agreeableness based on sexual orientation.

Analyses of residuals adjusted for age are presented in supplementary Table S1 and Table S2. For both men and women, they include KW tests for neuroticism, extraversion, and conscientiousness. In comparison with the main analyses, three differences in terms of the significance of the tested relationships arose for the male sample: The differences in neuroticism between bisexual and pansexual men (original d = 0.47, new d = 0.40), extraversion between heterosexual and asexual men (original d = 0.79, new d = 0.77), and conscientiousness between gay and pansexual men (original d = 0.43, new d = 0.35) were no longer significant when controlling for the effect of age.

For women, three of the above-reported differences in neuroticism were no longer significant; this pertains to comparisons of heterosexual to bisexual (original d = 0.13, new d = 0.07) and pansexual (original d = 0.15, new d = 0.09) women, as well as to comparisons of lesbian with asexual (original d = 0.31, new d = 0.23) women. Furthermore, the comparison between heterosexual and pansexual (original d = 0.24, new d = 0.18) and asexual (original d = 0.31, new d = 0.24) women, and between lesbian and bisexual (original d = 0.23, new d = 0.17) women in conscientiousness were no longer statistically significant when controlling for the effect of age.

DISCUSSION

Previous scholarship has established some differences in Big Five traits among individuals of various sexual orientations. In this large-scale online study, we aimed to replicate these previously established differences in a novel language and countries-Czechia and Slovakia. We found higher neuroticism in non-heterosexual men (when compared to their heterosexual counterparts) but not in women (once the age was controlled for), lower extraversion in asexual individuals, higher openness in bisexual and pansexual individuals (especially women), and mixed findings regarding conscientiousness. Finally, we found no differences in agreeableness across sexual orientations in both sexes. Our results fit well within those obtained by previous scholarship.

Our first prediction was supported, as we recorded higher neuroticism in nonheterosexual men-this is in line with both the minority stress theory and the gender shift framework, as well as with previous studies in gay, bisexual (Allen & Robson, 2020; Allen & Walter, 2018), and pansexual men (Junkins et al., 2024). Previous studies do not conclusively agree on the difference in neuroticism among women of different sexual orientations (Allen & Robson, 2020; Allen & Walter, 2018) or between asexual men and heterosexual men (Bogaert et al., 2018; Carvalho et al., 2017).

The minority stress theory serves as a prominent framework that could explain higher neuroticism in non-heterosexual people. Prejudice and discrimination that non-heterosexual individuals experience could be, apart from higher rates of suicidality and worse indicators of mental health (Meyer, 2003; Wittgens et al., 2022), reflected also in their higher neuroticism. Alternatively, higher scores in neuroticism in non-heterosexual men can be an epiphenomenon of the so-called gender shift (for details, see the Introduction and LeVay, 2017).

Since neuroticism is also defined as susceptibility to psychological vulnerability and, at the same time, there is a sex difference in neuroticism, with women scoring higher than men (Schmitt et al., 2008), our results for non-heterosexual men fit well within both the minority stress theory and the gender shift framework. Nonetheless, for women, these two frameworks provide different predictions: Non-heterosexual women should be higher than heterosexual women in neuroticism according to the minority stress theory and lower if the gender shift was in play. We believe these factors can interact, which could explain inconsistent results of previous studies regarding neuroticism in women. In the analyses where variation in age was partialed out, there were no differences between heterosexual and non-heterosexual women, however, lesbian women still scored statistically significantly lower in neuroticism than bisexual and pansexual women. It might be that lesbian women are more influenced by the gender shift than bisexual and pansexual women, who are (unlike lesbian women) susceptible to bi/pansexual-specific minority stress they experience from both heterosexual and gay/lesbian individuals (Feinstein et al., 2023; Mereish et al., 2017).

Additionally, Zietsch et al. (2011) found a genetic correlation between neuroticism and nonheterosexuality, while other studies (Ujma et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2023) reported a decrease in mental health disparities when non-heterosexual individuals are compared to their own heterosexual siblings (set against the case when they are compared to non-related heterosexuals), suggesting that shared familial influences, including genetics and shared familial environmental factors, can also affect the relationship between neuroticism and sexual orientation.

Our second prediction about higher openness in non-heterosexual men and women was supported only partially. Neither gay men nor lesbian women differed from their heterosexual counterparts in openness, which contrasts with the results of the two metaanalyses indicating higher openness in gay/lesbian individuals (Allen & Robson, 2020; Allen & Walter, 2018). Nevertheless, bisexual and pansexual men and women scored higher in openness than heterosexual individuals, which is in line with previous studies (Allen & Robson, 2020; Junkins et al., 2024). Bogaert et al. (2018) proposed that non-heterosexual people's unique experiences of already breaking social norms of expected heterosexuality may enable them to be more open and liberal also in other aspects of their psychological functioning. We speculate that homosexuality in Czechia and Slovakia might be nowadays far more accepted as a "mainstream" sexual orientation (unlike bisexuality or pansexuality), so the factor causing higher openness of gay/lesbian people found in previous studies may no longer be in action, at least in some communities. Yet, Bogaert et al. (2018) proposed another interpretation regarding the higher openness of bisexual individuals-only individuals who are open enough to explore their sexuality (and gain sexual experience with people of both sexes) may later identify as bisexual or pansexual.

Our third prediction concerning lower levels of extraversion in asexual men and women was supported-asexual individuals scored lower in extraversion in comparison with individuals of other sexual orientations, which again agrees with the results of previous studies so far (Bogaert et al., 2018; Carvalho et al., 2017; Greaves et al., 2021; Junkins et al., 2024). It is worth mentioning there was a strong sex-based bias in our sample of asexual people, the numbers of women exceeding the numbers of men (something that has been recorded also in probabilistic samples ; Bogaert, 2004; Rothblum et al., 2020). While the sample size of asexual women (N = 121) ensured sufficient power for pairwise comparisons, we point out a particularly small sample size of asexual men (N = 13), which considerably decreased the power of pairwise comparisons, albeit not for the key predicted extraversion difference.

A positive relationship between extraversion and variables associated with heightened sexual activity, including a higher number of sexual partners, was repeatedly reported (Eysenck, 1976; Rogowska et al., 2022). It is, therefore, possible that low extraversion underlies all these sexuality-related characteristics, including asexual identification-for example, low extraversion may lead to lower effort invested in meeting other people, which may, in turn, result in fewer options for initiating sexual relationships. Conversely, asexual individuals may report lower extraversion as a result of having less interest in initiating sex and socializing in order to obtain sexual partners.

Gay and bisexual men scored higher in conscientiousness than heterosexual men, which partly disagrees with two meta-analyses (Allen & Robson, 2020; Allen & Walter, 2018). Bisexual women scored lower than heterosexual and lesbian women and asexual and pansexual women scored lower than heterosexual women, which agrees with previous studies (Allen & Robson, 2020; Bogaert et al., 2018; Carvalho et al., 2017). Nonetheless, when age variation was partialed out, the only difference in conscientiousness that remained statistically significant was between bisexual and heterosexual women. Schmitt et al. (2008) reported a small sex difference (d = 0.12) in conscientiousness, with women scoring higher than men. Our results regarding a comparison of gay/lesbian and bisexual individuals with heterosexual people are in accordance with a gender shift phenomenon (but note that we found no significant difference between lesbian and heterosexual women). Lower conscientiousness in asexual women is difficult to interpret (Carvalho et al., 2017). It may be that people low in conscientiousness may generally be less able to maintain relationships (including sexual ones), as has been already shown for friendships and romantic relationships (Harris & Vazire, 2016), which could potentially contribute to their asexual identification.

Nonetheless, we emphasize that this is a speculative explanation and future research should specifically test this assertion.

We did not find a main effect of sexual orientation on agreeableness, neither in men nor in women. This aligns with meta-analyses of male samples (Allen & Robson, 2020; Allen & Walter, 2018), one study that utilized pansexual mixed-sex sample (Junkins et al., 2024) and three studies that included asexual men and women (Bogaert et al., 2018; Carvalho et al., 2017; Junkins et al., 2024 , but see Greaves et al., 2021). In contrast, the meta-analysis of female samples found lower agreeableness for both bisexual and lesbian women in comparison with heterosexual women (Allen & Robson, 2020, but see Allen & Walter, 2018). We currently have no solid explanation for why our results for women diverge from those of a meta-analysis, and future research should confirm the robustness of these findings.

The magnitude of the recorded differences is worth highlighting. The 100 individual d effect sizes range from 0.00 (multiple effect sizes) to 1.09 (extraversion difference between asexual and pansexual men), but most of them are to be conventionally described as trivial or small (d < 0.5; Cohen, 1988). Out of statistically significant results, notable exceptions include (i) lower extraversion in asexual individuals (ds = 0.72-1.09), (ii) higher openness in pansexual compared to heterosexual women (d = 0.50), and (iii) lower neuroticism in heterosexual compared to pansexual men (d = 0.66). In general, the magnitude of our results could be interpreted along the gender similarities hypothesis (Hyde, 2005), which has been recently expanded (Junkins et al., 2024 (Junkins et al., , 2025) ) to more broadly account also for differences across sexual orientations and gender minorities. In terms of the expanded version of the hypothesis, people with different sexual orientations or gender identities are more similar than dissimilar to each other in many psychological variables and most of the existing differences should be described as small at best. Overall, our results align well with this perspective, and although many of our bivariate relationships were statistically significant, only few (see above) could be interpreted at least as medium in terms of effect size.

Strengths and Limitations

The main strength of our study is a relatively large sample of almost 7,000 participants with a disproportionately high number of non-heterosexual participants, including also self-identified asexual and pansexual individuals. The inclusion of pansexual and asexual participants in studies on personality differences is rare, and we are aware of only two studies that did so (Junkins et al., 2024 (Junkins et al., , 2025)). Limitations include possible self-selection of our participants, which may have resulted in sampling bias that could have conceivably interfered with assessing some Big Five traits. Namely, we speculate that individuals who scored higher in openness could have been more likely to commence the survey, or individuals who scored higher in conscientiousness could have been more likely to complete the survey and provide more complete data. However, this limitation applies to any other online study that did not use incentives. Finally, as noted earlier, our project was publicly advertised as "Sexual orientation, personality, and attractiveness." We speculate that this may have led to self-selection of participants who were above-average satisfied with their physical appearance. Given the potential link between physical attractiveness and Big Five traits (Goldberg & Saucier, 1998), this may, in turn, have influenced the sample's mean Big Five scores. Another limitation pertains to the use of the short, 10-item form of BFI, which was selected as a trade-off between the number of scales used (see Supplementary Material) and the total length of the survey, which may impact the participant's attention and quality of the data. Reliability estimates for individual traits were generally at least acceptable only for neuroticism but rather low for other traits (see Measures). Nevertheless, these values are comparable to reliability estimates of BFI-10 gained in a Czech validation study, which also found generally acceptable correlations between BFI-10 and a more comprehensive, 44-item BFI-44 (ranging from r = .66 for agreeableness to r = .85 for neuroticism, mean r = .76; Hřebíčková et al., 2016).

CONCLUSION

In this online study, we tested the Big Five personality differences in a large sample of Czech and Slovak self-identified asexual, bisexual, heterosexual, gay/lesbian, and pansexual men and women. Our results largely agree with those obtained from previous studies-the most important including higher neuroticism in non-heterosexual men in general (compared to heterosexual men), higher openness to experience in bisexual and pansexual individuals (compared to their heterosexual and gay/lesbian counterparts of the same sex), and lower extraversion in asexual individuals (compared to individuals of other sexual orientations). Magnitude of the recorded differences was generally rather small. Various factors could contribute to these differences, including minority stress and other social experiences pertaining specifically to non-heterosexual individuals and common biological factors (genetics, prenatal sex hormones) underlying both sexual orientation and personality.

Our understanding of contribution of these factors is currently limited and should be targeted by future studies.
